In fact, I had no worries about her. She was what people call a capable woman and could manage her worldly affairs without my help. To tell the truth, I believe she always considered me an idle boy, a useless extra, fit only for building castles in the air, and was rather pleased to be rid of me. It was dark when I said goodbye. Taking along as my assistants the three creditors who had caused me so much trouble, we carried the balloon, its basket, and its equipment by an indirect route to the place where the remaining supplies were stored. We found everything undisturbed, and I immediately set to work.

“It was the first of April. As I have said, the night was dark, without a single visible star, and intermittent drizzle made us extremely uncomfortable. My principal concern, however, was the balloon. Despite its protective varnish, the moisture was beginning to make it rather heavy; the powder, too, was vulnerable to damage. I therefore kept my three debt collectors hard at work, packing ice around the central barrel and stirring the acid in the others. Nevertheless, they continually pestered me with questions about my intentions for all this equipment and complained bitterly about the dreadful labor I demanded of them. They could not see, they said, what benefit they might gain from getting soaked to the skin merely to participate in such horrible spells. I grew anxious and worked as hard as I could, for I truly believe the fools thought I had made a pact with the devil and that my present activities were, in short, thoroughly disreputable. I was consequently very afraid they would abandon me altogether. I managed to reassure them, though, by promising to settle every debt in full as soon as I had completed the business in hand. Naturally, they interpreted these remarks in their own way, no doubt imagining that somehow I would acquire an enormous quantity of ready cash. As long as I paid everything I owed, with a little extra for their services, I dare say they cared very little what became of either my soul or my body.

“After about four and a half hours, I found that the balloon was sufficiently inflated. I therefore attached the basket and loaded all my implements into it, taking care to include the condensing apparatus, a plentiful supply of water, and a large stock of provisions such as pemmican, which packs considerable nourishment into relatively little space.

“If not, and you ask for my patience and the mercy of those you have badly hurt, sit in that chair without another word. It has been waiting for you for two full days.”

Monks muttered something that could not be understood, but still hesitated.

“Decide quickly,” said Mr. Brownlow. “One word from me, and this choice will be gone forever.”

The man continued to hesitate.

“I have no wish to bargain,” said Mr. Brownlow. “And since I am protecting the most important interests of other people, I have no right to do so.”

“Is there—” Monks asked unsteadily, “is there no middle way?”

“None.”

Monks looked anxiously at the old gentleman. But his face showed only firmness and determination, so Monks entered the room, shrugged, and sat down.

“Lock the door from outside,” Mr. Brownlow told the men attending them, “and return when I ring.”

They obeyed, leaving the two men alone.

“This is fine treatment, sir,” Monks said, throwing down his hat and cloak, “from my father’s oldest friend.”

“It is because I was your father’s oldest friend, young man,” Mr. Brownlow replied. “It is because the hopes of my happy younger years were tied to him and to that lovely member of his family who died young, leaving me alone in the world. It is because, when he was still a boy, he knelt beside me at his only sister’s deathbed, on the morning when she would have become my wife if Heaven had not decided otherwise. From that day until his death, my wounded heart remained devoted to him through every hardship and mistake. Old memories fill my heart, and even seeing you makes me think of him again. For all these reasons I am willing to treat you gently now—yes, Edward Leeford, even now—and feel ashamed that you are so unworthy of the name you bear.”

“What does the name have to do with this?” the other man asked. He had watched his companion’s distress, partly in silence and partly with stubborn bewilderment. “What does that name mean to me?”

“Nothing,” said Mr. Brownlow. “Nothing to you. But it was hers. Even after all these years, I still feel the warmth and excitement that once came over me simply at hearing a stranger say it. I am very glad you changed it—very, very glad.”

“This is all very fine,” said Monks, to keep using his assumed name. A long silence had passed, during which he had shifted about in sullen defiance while Mr. Brownlow sat with his hand covering his face.

The mental qualities we describe as analytical do not readily lend themselves to analysis. We recognize them chiefly through their effects. Among other things, we know that people who possess these qualities to an exceptional degree invariably find them a source of intense pleasure. Just as a strong man rejoices in his physical strength and enjoys exercises that engage his muscles, the analyst delights in the mental activity of unraveling a problem. Even the most trivial pursuits give him pleasure if they bring his talent into use. He enjoys puzzles, riddles, and hieroglyphics, displaying in their solutions a perceptiveness that strikes an ordinary observer as almost supernatural. His conclusions, reached through the very essence of methodical reasoning, actually have every appearance of intuition.

The ability to resolve problems may be greatly strengthened by studying mathematics, particularly its highest branch, which has been unfairly granted the distinctive name of analysis merely because it works backward. Yet calculation is not, in itself, analysis. A chess player, for instance, calculates without making an effort to analyze. The influence of chess on the mind is therefore widely misunderstood. I am not writing a formal treatise, only introducing a rather unusual narrative with some loosely connected observations. I will thus venture to say that the higher powers of reflective thought are exercised more effectively and usefully by the modest game of draughts than by all the elaborate frivolity of chess. In chess, the pieces have different, peculiar movements and values that vary with circumstances. Mere complexity is mistaken for profundity, a fairly common error. The game makes considerable demands on attention. If that attention slips for an instant, a mistake follows, producing a disadvantage or defeat. Because the possible moves are both numerous and intricate, the opportunities for such errors multiply. In nine cases out of ten, the winner is the player with greater concentration rather than greater insight. In draughts, by contrast, the moves are uniform and offer little variation, so accidental oversights are less likely. With simple attention relatively unoccupied, any advantage either player gains must come from superior perceptiveness. To put this more concretely, imagine a game of draughts reduced to four kings, where no careless mistake can reasonably be expected. Clearly, assuming the players are reasonably evenly matched, victory can come only through an unusually subtle move, one produced by a powerful effort of thought.
